title: Multicatalyst reactions induce abrupt transition in a dense catalytic reaction network model
abstract: We generalize the Furusawa--Kaneko model, a simple model of intracellular catalytic reaction networks, to multicatalyst reactions and analyze the generalized model using dynamical mean-field theory. In the thermodynamic and dense-network limit, we derive exact effective equations and analyze their fixed points for arbitrary degree distributions. Under nutrient-poor conditions, network heterogeneity suppresses the metabolic--starvation transition irrespective of the number of catalysts per reaction. In contrast, under nutrient-rich conditions, the bifurcation structure changes with the number of catalysts. With one catalyst per reaction, only continuous transitions occur, whereas two or more catalysts give rise to bistable phases and discontinuous transitions. The bifurcation structure also differs between two and three catalysts per reaction, with three catalysts allowing bistability between metabolic states with different cell growth rates. Our results provide a possible mechanism for bistability and abrupt switching in metabolic dynamics.
summary: This work models intracellular metabolism using a generalized catalytic network incorporating multiple catalysts per reaction. By applying Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, the authors show that increasing the number of catalysts fundamentally changes the system's stability, inducing abrupt, discontinuous transitions and bistability under nutrient-rich conditions. This provides a theoretical mechanism for sudden metabolic switching in biological systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates how introducing multicatalyst reactions into a dense catalytic network model alters the metabolic dynamics, specifically looking for mechanisms causing abrupt transitions and bistability.
main_result: The introduction of two or more catalysts per reaction leads to the emergence of bistable phases and discontinuous transitions under nutrient-rich conditions, a feature absent in simpler models.
method: The analysis employs Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) to derive effective equations for the network in the thermodynamic and dense-network limits, followed by bifurcation analysis.
model_or_system: The system is a generalized Furusawa–Kaneko model describing intracellular catalytic reaction networks, involving species categorized as catalytic and nutrient groups. Dynamics include reaction kinetics, nutrient uptake, and cell growth/dilution.
key_observables: Bifurcation structure, presence of bistable phases, and the nature of phase transitions (continuous vs. discontinuous).

main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the dense-connectivity and thermodynamic limits, and assumes catalytic species are unpenetrable.

paper_structure: The paper generalizes the model, derives effective equations using DMFT, and then analyzes the fixed points and bifurcation structure under varying nutrient and catalyst conditions to characterize the transition types.
why_interesting: While focused on biochemistry, the use of DMFT and bifurcation analysis to study non-equilibrium phase transitions in complex interacting systems shares methodological overlap with analyzing many-body dynamics in open quantum systems.
